::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[find the quotient space $\mathbb{M}(n;\mathbb{R})/\mathbb{T}(n;\mathbb{R})$, upto isomoprhism](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2543047/find-the-quotient-space-mathbbmn-mathbbr-mathbbtn-mathbbr-upt), asked by [QED](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/91884/qed) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2017-11-29; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> Let $\mathbb{T}(n;\mathbb{R})\subset\mathbb{M}(n;\mathbb{R})$ denote the set of all matrices whose trace is zero. How do I 
>
> > find the quotient space
> > $\mathbb{M}(n;\mathbb{R})/\mathbb{T}(n;\mathbb{R})$, upto isomoprhism?
>
>  As much as I have understood $\mathbb{M}(n;\mathbb{R})\cong\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$, and as for any matrix in $\mathbb{T}(n;\mathbb{R})$, the one of the diagonal element will be determined by the sum of the rest of the diagonal elements, $\mathbb{T}(n;\mathbb{R})\cong\mathbb{R}^{n^2-1}$. Hence the quotient space $\mathbb{M}(n;\mathbb{R})/\mathbb{T}(n;\mathbb{R})\cong\mathbb{R}^{n^2}/\mathbb{R}^{n^2-1}\cong\mathbb{R}$.
>
> Have I done it right?
:::

I'm not quite sure what you mean by “find”, but yes, the quotient space is one-dimensional.  

The trace itself is a linear map from your $\mathbb{M}(n;\mathbb{R})$ onto $\mathbb{R}$.  Its kernel or nullspace is, by definition, $\mathbb{T}(n;\mathbb{R})$.  So by the [first isomorphism theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isomorphism_theorems#First_isomorphism_theorem_3),
$$\mathbb{M}(n;\mathbb{R})/\mathbb{T}(n;\mathbb{R}) \cong \mathbb{R}$$
